E1286.summary: In Proclus as reported by Atwood, the soul's undefiled union with the Father, in which it rests established in him as in a harbour.
E1286.body: A term Atwood reports from Proclus: “This, then, is the Paternal Port and the discovery of the Father, according to Proclus, viz., an undefiled union with him” [II.4 ¶41]. The image is of “locating the soul in the Father, as in a port” [II.4 ¶41]. So the text itself identifies the Paternal Port with undefiled union with the Father.

E1287.summary: In the Appendix, Atwood's name for the seed of this life, which is said to be drawn up.
E1287.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood equates the paternal principle with the seed of life: “The seed of this life, the paternal principle, is drawn up.” [APP ¶98]. The text gives no further explanation here.

E1288.summary: That which Intellect seeks in the allegory of the descent, according to Atwood.
E1288.body: Atwood reads the allegory of the descent as “an inquiry of Intellect after its Paternal Source” [II.3 ¶13]. The context suggests the term names the origin to which Intellect seeks to return. The text does not define it further.

E1289.summary: Paired with 'agent': that in which the agent's sin is multiplied and lives on in the 'unhappy offspring'.
E1289.body: Atwood uses 'patient' as the counterpart of 'agent'. The records show it as that in which the agent's sin is multiplied, so that “it should survive in the unhappy offspring unto the third or fourth generation” [IV.3 ¶56]. The text does not define the term further here.

E1290.summary: In Eudoxus, the leaven needed to ferment the Stone in the Fifth Key.
E1290.body: Eudoxus speaks here, quoted by Atwood: “the Perfect Body is a necessary leaven of Our Paste” [IV.3 ¶14]. So the text identifies the Perfect Body with the leaven of Our Paste, the leaven by which the Stone is fermented in the Fifth Key.

E1291.summary: In the Author of the Open Entrance, the matter joined with the Mercury of the First Work in the Multiplication.
E1291.body: This comes from the Author of the Open Entrance, quoted by Atwood. In the Multiplication one is told to “take one part of the Perfect Matter” [IV.3 ¶18] and join it with the Mercury of the First Work. The term is not defined further here.

E1292.summary: Whitened water made red by conjunction with its own permanent prepared spirit; its Art is called 'our brass'.
E1292.body: In a footnote, Atwood gives the reddening of the whitened water: “By a conjunction with its own permanent prepared spirit, the albified water is made red” [I.3 n54]. The same note links the Art of the permanent water with 'our brass'.

E1293.summary: In the Appendix, the Divine line in all things, which withdraws from sense in mesmerizing, as opposed to the transverse line.
E1293.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says: “The perpendicular line is the Divine line in all things” [APP ¶13]. In mesmerizing it withdraws from sense. Were it stronger in us than the transverse line, we would no longer be in sense [APP ¶13].

E1294.summary: In the Appendix, the magnetism ('altitude') that dissolves the sensuous vehicle, freeing the soul and moving consciousness into another medium.
E1294.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says that Perpendicular Magnetism dissolves the sensuous vehicle and moves consciousness into another medium: “By the former the soul is set free” [APP ¶173]. It is linked with 'altitude'. The context suggests it is set against another, contrasting kind of magnetism.

E1295.summary: Ancient lamps found still burning in tombs and urns, which Atwood takes as proof that the Romans knew chemistry and the occult laws of light.
E1295.body: Atwood describes ancient lamps found still burning in tombs and urns, kept alight by a pure liquor. She treats them as evidence: “the perpetual lamps best prove, and without offence, that the Romans understood something of chemistry and the occult laws of light” [I.1 ¶18].

E1296.summary: Thorough, searching investigation: the means by which reason proves all things, and something the stiff-necked lack.
E1296.body: Two voices use the word. Geber, quoted by Atwood, describes the stiff-necked as “void of ingenuity and every sort of perscrutination” [III.4 ¶3]. Atwood herself makes it reason's task: “It is the province of reason to inquire and endeavor, by perscrutination, to prove all things” [III.4 ¶15]. In her method, then, searching inquiry is required, and its absence disqualifies.

E1297.summary: Hermes' name for the searching inner fire or secret sulfur that stirs up and purifies the matter; Atwood identifies it with the investigating Intellect that works the change.
E1297.body:
In a footnote, Atwood, citing Hermes, describes a secret sulfur: “It is the stirrer-up of the whole power and efficacy and purifier of the matter; hence Hermes calls it the Perscrutinator” [I.3 n32]. Hermes calls this temperate unguent or fire 'the Perscrutinator of the water'. Atwood adds that it is what is “eminently distinguishing the Rational Ferment” [I.3 n32].

In III.1 she takes the term inward. It is “that same perscrutinating Intellect which Hermes speaks of” [III.1 ¶21], the searching intellect that brings about the whole change. The sequestration that gives form and essence belongs to it [III.1 ¶21]. She also equates it with Eirenaeus' phrase: “It is this vital perscrutinator, the internal fire of the sulfur of thy water, as Eirenaeus calls it” [III.1 ¶13].

Asserted identities: the secret sulfur [I.3 n32]; the internal fire of the sulfur of thy water [III.1 ¶13]; the perscrutinating Intellect [III.1 ¶21].

forms: Perseus, Theseus, Bacchus, Ulysses, Hercules, Jason
E1298.summary: Heroes Atwood cites together: their labors before reward illustrate the toil needed to gain Wisdom.
E1298.body: Atwood names these heroes together. Their labors come before their reward, and she uses this to show the toil required for Wisdom [IV.1 ¶25].

E1301.summary: Author of an epistle addressed to Artaxerxes, cited for its account of Hippocrates' divine nature and healing.
E1301.body: Atwood cites an epistle by Petris, the Persian, addressed to Artaxerxes. It tells of Hippocrates' divine nature and healing: “this man is the prince of divine knowledge” [IV.3 ¶32]. See also [IV.3 ¶34]. The footnote points to Helmont, Tumulus Pestis [IV.3 n12]. Atwood uses the epistle as illustration.

E1303.summary: In the Appendix, a region passed before entering the world's solution, after which the inner vision is the same for all.
E1303.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says that the inner vision is the same for all “after they have passed the phantasmagoric region” [APP ¶144] and entered the world's solution. The text does not explain the term further.

E1304.summary: Figured images produced by the mind's own fancy, or by nature and the demiurgic intellect, as distinct from the gods' true self-manifestation.
E1304.body: Atwood separates phantasms from the gods' true self-manifestation. Phantasms are figured images that come from the mind's own fancy, or from nature and the demiurgic intellect. She speaks of the case “if various phantasms are hurled forth before the presence of them” [II.4 ¶29].

E1305.summary: The imaginative spirit, the natural vehicle of our life and the vestibule of Reason; confusing and possessive while impure, it can be purified and refined by Intellect.
E1305.body:
In II.2 Atwood describes the imaginative spirit in man and animals. While impure it produces a 'phantastic life' and confusion and possession of the mind, and it is likened to the Sphinx: “such is said to be the nature of the Phantastic Spirit before it is mundified” [II.2 ¶15]. It can be cleansed: “But the phantastic Spirit may be purified, even in brutes” [II.2 ¶13]. She links it with what Iamblicus calls the mundane spirit: “Thus Iamblicus, speaking of this mundane spirit, says” [II.2 ¶15].

In III.1 she places it in the soul's anatomy: “the Phantastic Spirit, which is the natural vehicle of our life” [III.1 ¶5]. She also links it to the natural intelligent Spirit: “for what the natural intelligent Spirit is in man, that Ether is in the universe; and this intelligence, phantasic as it is and drawn without, may be called the vestibule of Reason” [III.1 ¶5].

Synesius, as Atwood quotes him, gives Intellect the work of purifying it: “Intellect above all things separates whatever is contrary to the true purity of phantastic Spirit” [III.1 ¶20]. Intellect thins it and extends it toward Divinity. The text does not say it is the same as the Ethereal Spirit.

Asserted identities: mundane spirit [II.2 ¶15]; natural vehicle of our life [III.1 ¶5]; natural intelligent Spirit [III.1 ¶5].

E1306.summary: The imagination: a region of notions and instincts that hinders intellectual conception and, if it prevails, turns the inner life to folly.
E1306.body:
Olympiodorus, quoted by Atwood, calls it a hindrance: “The phantasy, says he, is an impediment to our intellectual conception” [II.2 ¶12]. He also sets it against enthusiasm.

The ancients, as she reports them, describe “the region of the phantasy, with its notions and instincts” [II.2 ¶22]. Its contents are often more false, fleeting and evil than sense images, and it is dangerous to dwell in passively.

In her own voice, Atwood counts phantasy as a mode of the One Thing, alongside folly and passion: “the phantasy, if suffered to prevail, will convert all to her own folly in the internal life” [III.1 ¶21]. Once phantasy is subdued, the Ethereal Spirit abandons it.

E1307.summary: Religious groups Atwood names together in the Appendix as examples of religious self-will in history.
E1307.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood names these groups as historical examples of religious self-will [APP ¶110].

E1309.summary: 'The Jew Philo', whom Atwood cites for the rational part of man as God's temple and the soul as the impression of the Logos-seal.
E1309.body:
Atwood cites Philo in support of two points: that the rational part of man is God's temple, and that the soul bears the impression of the Logos-seal. “God dwells, says the Jew Philo, in the rational part of man as in a palace” [II.1 ¶43]. The works named in her footnotes are De Praemiis et Poenis, De Nobilitate, De Profugis and De Plantatione Noe [II.1 n39, II.1 n40].

Elsewhere she lists Philo-Judaeus with Plotinus, Proclus, Porphyry, Jamblicus, Julian and Apuleius. These are Alexandrian revival figures who professed Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge, and she says she will quote them later [I.1 ¶27].

E1310.summary: An unnamed 'philosopher' cited throughout the book for a range of maxims on the work, the soul and illumination, usually in support of Atwood's points.
E1310.body:
The phrase 'the philosopher' stands for an unnamed authority at many points. The text does not show that it is always the same person.

- Within Hermes' text, the philosopher is cited for the permanent works [I.3 ¶30] and for the Botri saying: “Botri is made from the Citrine” [I.3 ¶41].
- On the soul, citing Plotinus's Select Works (Taylor, page 387) in a footnote: “When the soul is situated in the body, says the philosopher, she departs from self-contemplation” [II.1 ¶50, II.1 n44]. The point supported is that the purified soul recollects what it forgot.
- “Dimidium facti qui bene coepit habet” [III.1 ¶24], i.e. (ours) a good beginning is half the work.
- On the Night of Matter: “By no means, says the philosopher” [III.2 ¶55]. Here the point is that the mind receives the formless rather than understanding nothing.
- The worker should work faithfully until it be the Divine pleasure to make the work appear [III.3 ¶80].
- On the Gordian Knot: “who is he that is bale to untie it, enquires the philosopher?” [IV.1 ¶37].
- “Labor to know causes” [IV.1 ¶44]. Atwood endorses this as the condition of success.
- On self-preparation, invitation and sudden illumination: “Fit thy roof to thy God in all thou canst” [IV.2 ¶39, IV.2 ¶41].

E1311.summary: Genuine seekers of the Stone, as against knaves and sordid chemists; the disciplined, proven person to whom alone Nature gives up her casket.
E1311.body: Atwood separates true philosophers from impostors. Experiments went on in secret “both by knaves and philosophers” [I.1 ¶55], and the philosopher stands apart from idlers and 'sordid chemists'. In her account Nature gives her secret only to the qualified: “she will surrender to none but a philosopher, one too that has been disciplined in her schools” [III.4 ¶13]. That is someone tried and proven able to bear the sacred trust.

E1312.summary: The adepts as a group, cited for doctrines on the First Matter, gold, and spirit and body; Atwood also notes they are silent on key preparations.
E1312.body:
Atwood cites 'the philosophers' as a group for several doctrines:

- The First Matter is sought inwardly: “The First Matter is not to be found on earth, as the philosophers say” [APP ¶137] (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer).
- As Hermes reports, they praise gold: “this gold, in relation of other bodies, is as the sun amongst the stars” [I.3 ¶58].
- Spirit and body must be joined for generation: “the Spirit is Eve, the Body is Adam” [IV.3 ¶7].
- In ancient times they dug out the saving Salt and exalted it by circulating media [IV.4 ¶20].

She also points out their limits. None of them shows how to obtain the two mercuries. They pass over that point 'very slightly' and treat the preparation of Mercury 'in silence'. The Adepts say more about the last operations than about the First, so reading them alone will hardly suffice [IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶14, IV.3 ¶16].

E1313.summary: Authorities cited within Norton's verse on working 'within locks nyne' and on the importance of a fitting place.
E1313.body: These authorities speak inside Norton's verse, which Atwood quotes: “Philosophers said, by their engine, How it should be wrought within locks nyne” [III.4 ¶41]. The passage also stresses how much a fitting place matters for the work.

E1314.summary: Not common gold but a living, luminous, purified substance that ripens and perfects other bodies; also the transmuting powder in Van Helmont's projection.
E1314.body:
In Van Helmont's account, quoted by Atwood, it is a transmuting powder: he projected “one grain of the philosophers’ gold upon some thousands of grains of boiling quicksilver” [I.1 ¶76]. In Khunrath's words it is identified with “the blood of the Lion, which is the gold of the philosophers” [I.1 ¶81]. It may also be read as the universal tincture; the text leaves this open.

Atwood's own account, drawing on the adepts, makes it a living substance, not metal: “Our gold is not common gold, says the adept, but a depurated substance” [I.3 n63]. It has a heavenly complexion, and it ripens and perfects other bodies. Paradoxically “the gold of the wise is more heavy than lead” [I.3 ¶61], and it is made into Ixir with a fiery water.

Asserted identities: living gold, “The gold of the philosophers, or living gold, as they sometimes call their luminous concrete” [I.3 n65]; our earth, “our earth is gold” [I.3 ¶62]; the blood of the Lion [I.1 ¶81].

E1315.summary: Earlier authorities criticized inside a quoted poem for describing the making of Magnesia while hiding imbibition.
E1315.body: Inside a poem Atwood quotes, the 'Philosophers of tyme old' or 'olde Fathers' are faulted for describing the creation of Magnesia while concealing imbibition: “The secret of Imbibition never out tould;” [III.1 ¶65].

E1316.summary: The body of the work, which carries a shadowy darkness with it until it is purified of sensual defilements.
E1316.body: Atwood writes in a footnote: “A shadowy darkness passes always along with the philosophic body” [I.3 n21]. The darkness stays with it until the body is purified of sensual defilements.

E1317.summary: In Eudoxus, a purely natural calcination of the Stone that sublimes and distills it and increases its radical humidity, unlike destructive common calcination by fire.
E1317.body: Eudoxus, quoted by Atwood, calls it “a philosophic calcination which is purely natural” [IV.3 ¶16]. He contrasts it with common calcination by violence of fire, which destroys the body: “this philosophical calcination, which sublimes and distills the Stone in calcining it, much augments its humidity” [IV.3 ¶16]. It preserves and increases the Stone's radical humidity.

E1318.summary: In Eirenaeus, things whose exact preparation is the first degree of perfection in the Art; not explained further.
E1318.body: Eirenaeus, quoted by Atwood, says: “the exact preparation of the philosophic Eagles may be considered the first degree of perfection in this Art” [IV.1 ¶11]. The text does not explain what the Eagles are.

E1319.summary: The process in which Life's substance is wholly transmuted, its threefold property developed and the forms of the Medial Spirit put out, followed by radical destruction and New Generation.
E1319.body: Atwood writes: “as Life passes through the philosophic fermentation, its substance is entirely transmuted” [III.2 ¶28]. In this process the threefold property of Life is developed and its heterogeneous parts are divided. The forms of the Medial Spirit are extinguished, and a radical destruction and a New Generation follow [III.2 ¶28].
